t: Newton derived Kepler's laws of planetary motion from an inverse square law of force and showed that the law applied across the Solar System, in the moon's motion, the tides, comets and the precession of the equinoxes.
The book began as a nine-page tract sent to Edmond Halley in 1684, grew over about two years of concentrated work, and was published in 1687 at Halley's own expense.
Its mathematics was accepted readily, but a force acting at a distance drew criticism from Huygens and Leibniz, and Newton answered with Hypotheses non fingo.
dyk: Between May 1684 and April 1686 Newton's chemical notebooks have no entries at all, though he had long kept dated notes of his experiments, which suggests that he did very little else for well over a year and a half.
ev: Newton studies colliding bodies and shows, for circular planetary motion, an inverse-square relation of force to distance
Newton sends Halley the nine-page tract De motu corporum in gyrum
The first book is presented to the Royal Society, Hooke makes a priority claim and Pepys gives his imprimatur
The complete Principia is published by Halley
The second edition appears under the editorship of Roger Cotes, with the General Scholium added
The third edition is published, with Rule 4 of the Rules of Reasoning
A new census of owners of the first edition identifies 387 copies

f.made: Isaac Newton, who wrote it from 1684 after Edmond Halley's visit; Halley saw it through the press and paid for the first edition at his own financial risk
f.form: A Latin work in three books, preceded by definitions and the axioms or laws of motion; argued in geometrical propositions, with later editions in 1713 and 1726
f.where: Copies of the first edition are held by libraries including Cambridge University Library, which has Newton's own annotated copy, and the Huntington Library, which has another copy of his with his notes
f.known: The laws of motion; the law of universal gravitation; an explanation of Kepler's laws of planetary motion; the Rules of Reasoning in Philosophy; the General Scholium and Hypotheses non fingo; the dispute with Hooke
